newsitem.title: MALTA: Euro-dispute spurs Malta election campaign.
newsitem.headline: Euro-dispute spurs Malta election campaign.

text.p: Like the island, Malta's electorate is tiny and political parties on Monday start their last full week of campaigning knowing that every vote matters in the October 26 general election.
Elections are traditionally close on the Mediterranean tourist island. Proposed membership of the European Union has added a cutting edge to the contest.
The ruling Nationalist Party of 62-year-old Prime Minister Eddie Fenech Adami, in power since 1987, espouses membership of the EU and has applied to join.
Its main opposition, a Labour Party led since 1992 by economist Alfred Sant, 66, is against, seeking instead close links based on an industrial free trade zone with the bloc.

A wild card is the small political grouping, Democratic Alternative, whose coordinator is Saviour Balzan. It failed to win seats in its first contest in 1992 but argues now that it will tackle subjects like the introduction of divorce, ignored by the two others.
Fenech Adami goes to the polls boosted by an economy growing at some six percent a year and a record unemployment low of some 3.2 percent.
"There is no Maltese who is not enjoying a better quality of life than nine years ago," Fenech Adami said when presenting his party programme to the 275,000 electorate.
"We are the party which has brought peace of mind, created unequalled job, educational and investment opportunities."

Sant argues that EU rules are unsuited to Malta and has promised to remove VAT (Value Added Tax), introduced on non-essential goods at a uniform 15 percent last year. He says it was imposed only to prepare Malta for EU membership.
He blames VAT for inflation and Labour promises to recoup revenue by re-introducing a customs system previously in place.

The Nationalists won a three-seat majority in the 65-seat parliament at re-election in 1992. At mass rallies and on election posters they project themselves as the party that brought serenity after 16 often stormy years of socialism.
The party boasts of better living standards, modernisation of the administration, an eight-fold rise in university student numbers, and a drop in income tax, despite introducing VAT.

The Nationalist government has also conducted an economic restructuring programme in line with EU directives, creating conditions for foreign banks to open and an infrastructure to convert the island into an international financial centre.
Malta applied to join the EU in 1990 and has been promised formal talks on membership six months after the end of the current EU inter-governmental conference.

Sant, who has never held government office, has promised to take Malta out of the NATO Partnership for Peace programme, which the island joined in 1995, saying is not in keeping with the island's neutrality and non-alignment status.
His Labour Party insists it has changed former restrictive policies on trade, the private sector and banking.
"The Labour Party has geared itself to the future, updating its policies to meet the people's aspirations while always putting the citizen first," Sant told a news conference.
Both leaders are touring towns and villages to get their message across, while some 300 candidates call on households and hold street parties.
